description: In mahāvedha the breath leaves the two side channels and throbs in the middle; the union of moon, sun and fire arises and a death-like state (mṛtāvasthā) appears before the breath is released.

For the practitioner of mahāmudrā nothing is wholesome or unwholesome; all tastes become tasteless and even terrible poison is digested like nectar; consumption, skin disease, constipation, gulma and indigestion disappear (the text's claims).
After six months of the inverted practice wrinkles and grey hair are no longer seen; the digestive fire grows so that ample food is needed (the text's claims).
Practised, the inner sound covers outer sound; within a fortnight the yogin overcomes all distraction and is happy; at first many loud sounds are heard, then subtler and subtler ones.

With khecarī, where the tongue meets the skull-cavity it tastes in turn salty, alkaline, bitter and astringent flavours, then butter, ghee, milk, curds, buttermilk, honey, grape-juice and nectar; hunger, thirst, swoon and sloth do not arise (the text's claims about a restricted practice).

In the nocturnal bhrāmarī the sounds heard in the right ear are first like crickets, then flute, thunder, the hum of bees, bell, gong, trumpet, kettle-drum, mṛdaṅga, vīṇā and dundubhi; within the resonance of the unstruck sound is a light, within the light the mind, which dissolves there.
In mūrcchā, with the mind set between the brows and all objects abandoned, a swoon of the mind arises that gives happiness; joining the mind to the self, various blisses arise daily.

The powers claimed for the five element-concentrations: going to and from the heavens in this body, moving as swiftly as mind; not dying by earth, water, fire or wind; moving in the sky; for the space-concentration, the opening of the door of liberation.
By the practice of trāṭaka śāmbhavī surely arises; eye diseases do not occur and divine sight is given.
By daily cleaning of the ear-openings the inner sound becomes manifest.

In yoni mudrā the practitioner, full of the power, delights in the supreme self with the sentiment of love, becomes full of bliss and one with Brahman — 'I am Brahman' — and non-dual samādhi arises; one established in it even once is in samādhi.

When the six openings are closed with the fingers and the breath restrained, the yogin sees the self as light; whoever sees it even for a moment is freed of sins; by constant practice he forgets the body and becomes one with it.

The first inner sound is like intoxicated bees, flute and vīṇā; then like a bell; then like the rumble of clouds; setting the mind fearlessly on it, laya arises and the mind is stilled with the sound.
With the tongue at the root of the palate and attention on the pit of the throat, hunger and thirst cease; attention on the kūrma-channel below it gives great steadiness of mind.

The ten forms of the unstruck sound in the Nādānusandhāna tract: ciṇī, ciñciṇī, ciri, conch, strings, a ringing, bronze cymbals, cloud, roaring water and the kettle-drum; the first nine are to be left, the tenth gives liberation.
